text.en: What happens to the product 23 × 27 if one number goes up by 1? And if one goes up by 1 and the other goes down by 1?

Algebra writes general statements compactly, and distributivity relates multiplication and addition: a(b + c) = ab + ac.
If 27 grows to 28, the product 23 × 27 grows by 23, because 23 × 28 = 23 × 27 + 23.
We usually skip the multiplication sign before brackets, so a(b + c) means a × (b + c).
The same property holds on the other side: (a + b)c = ac + bc.
If a is increased by 1 and b decreased by 1, the product (a + 1)(b − 1) expands to ab − a + b − 1.
So the product changes by b − a − 1; with a = 23 and b = 27 it increases by 3.
Special cases give identities: (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b² and (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b².
Also (a + b)(a − b) = a² − b², which lets us calculate 51 × 49 as 50² − 1² = 2,499.
Common mistakes: (a + b)² is not a² + b², and −(a − b) is −a + b, not −a − b.
Algebra gives many ways to reach the same answer, and checking with numbers tells us if a rule is right.

why.en: Pick numbers around a friendly base.

prompt.en: A friend says (a + b)² = a² + b². How do you reply?

requiredIdeas.en: So the middle term 2ab is missing.

points.en: a(b + c) = ab + ac and (a + b)c = ac + bc.
(a ± b)² = a² ± 2ab + b² and (a + b)(a − b) = a² − b².
Check rules with numbers to avoid mistakes.
